title: Poder vs Saber: How to Say “Can” in Spanish
seo_title: Poder vs Saber: How to Say “Can” in Spanish
meta_description: Poder vs saber: saber is can as a learned skill, poder is can as ability, possibility or permission. Clear rules, examples, common mistakes and a quiz.
excerpt: Can you swim, or can you swim today? Spanish uses two verbs for “can”.

body_html:
Poder vs saber is a subtle pair, because both can translate as “can”. Saber + infinitive means you know how to do something, a learned skill. Poder + infinitive means you are able to do it right now, or are allowed to, or it is possible. So a swimmer with a broken arm says Sé nadar, pero hoy no puedo: I can swim (I know how), but I can’t today.

Quick answer
  • Saber + infinitive = can (learned skill): Sé manejar.
  • Poder + infinitive = can (physical ability, circumstances): No puedo ir.
  • Poder = may, be allowed: ¿Puedo entrar?
  • Poder = possibility: Puede llover.
{{toc}}

Poder vs saber: the core rule

SaberPoder
Meaningto know how toto be able to, be allowed to
Depends onLearning, trainingCircumstances, strength, permission
ExampleSé hablar alemán. I can speak German.No puedo hablar ahora. I can’t talk now.

The RAE dictionary defines poder as having the ability or the opportunity to do something, while saber with an infinitive means having the skill to do it.

When to use saber for “can”

  • ¿Sabes nadar? Can you swim?
  • Mi abuela no sabe usar el celular. My grandmother can’t use a phone.
  • Sé tocar la guitarra. I can play the guitar.
  • Los niños ya saben leer. The children can read now.

If you could answer “I learned it”, use saber.

When to use poder

Ability in the moment or physical capacity

  • No puedo abrir la botella. I can’t open the bottle.
  • Con este ruido no puedo dormir. I can’t sleep with this noise.
  • ¿Puedes ver la pantalla? Can you see the screen?

Permission

  • ¿Puedo sentarme aquí? Can I sit here?
  • Aquí no se puede fumar. You can’t smoke here.

Possibility

  • Puede que llegue tarde. I might be late (with the subjunctive).
  • Eso no puede ser. That can’t be.

Requests

¿Puedes ayudarme? (Can you help me?) / ¿Podría traerme la cuenta? (Could you bring me the check?) The conditional podría is the polite form; see {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

The same activity, two verbs

SaberPoder
Sé manejar. I can drive (I have a license).No puedo manejar, tomé. I can’t drive, I’ve been drinking.
Sé cocinar. I can cook.Hoy no puedo cocinar, no hay gas. I can’t cook today, there’s no gas.
Sabe nadar. She can swim.No puede nadar, está resfriada. She can’t swim, she has a cold.
{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Can see, can hear: no verb needed

English often adds “can” to verbs of perception. Spanish usually doesn’t: ¿Me oyes? (Can you hear me?), No veo nada (I can’t see anything). ¿Puedes oírme? is also correct, but less common. More in {{link:oir-vs-escuchar|oír vs escuchar}}.

Conjugation note

Poder changes o → ue: puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden; preterite pude, pudo; conditional podría. In the preterite, pude often means “I managed to”, and no pude “I failed to”: Al final pude dormir (In the end I managed to sleep).

Real conversations

  • A: ¿Sabes esquiar? (Can you ski?)
  • B: Sí, sé esquiar, pero este invierno no puedo: me operaron de la rodilla. (Yes, I can ski, but I can’t this winter: I had knee surgery.)
  • A: ¡Vaya! ¿Puedo ayudarte en algo? (Oh no! Can I help you with anything?)

A quick mental shortcut

Imagine someone asks you the question on a job application. “Can you drive?” on a form is about a skill you have learned, so Spanish asks ¿Sabe manejar? Now imagine a friend asks the same question at the end of a party. That is about whether you are able to drive right now, so they ask ¿Puedes manejar? If the answer would still be true next month, it is probably saber; if it depends on today, it is poder.

Regional notes

The rule is the same across the Spanish-speaking world. One difference you will notice is how often people use the plain verb instead: ¿Hablas inglés? and ¿Nadas? are very common ways to ask about skills, and they avoid the choice altogether. In polite requests, ¿Me puede…? with usted is standard everywhere, while in Spain you will also hear ¿Me pones un café?, a direct present tense that sounds friendly rather than rude there.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
¿Puedes nadar? (asking about skill)¿Sabes nadar?Learned skill
No sé venir mañana.No puedo venir mañana.Circumstances
¿Sé ir al baño?¿Puedo ir al baño?Permission
Sé cómo manejar.Sé manejar.No cómo for skills
Puedo hablar español (meaning I know it)Sé hablar español / Hablo españolSkill: saber, or just the verb
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. Can you dance salsa? (¿Sabes bailar salsa?)
  2. I can’t go out tonight. (No puedo salir esta noche.)
  3. May I use your phone? (¿Puedo usar tu teléfono?)
  4. My son can already write his name. (Mi hijo ya sabe escribir su nombre.)
  5. It might rain tomorrow. (Puede que llueva mañana.)

Saber has another partner: {{link:saber-vs-conocer|saber vs conocer}}. For more pairs, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Ask whether the “can” is about learning or about circumstances. Learned skill: saber. Ability right now, permission or possibility: poder. And remember you can know how to do something perfectly and still not be able to do it today.

faq.q: What is the difference between poder and saber?
faq.a: Saber + infinitive means can in the sense of a learned skill (sé nadar). Poder means can in the sense of physical ability, circumstances, permission or possibility (no puedo nadar hoy).

faq.q: How do you say “Can you swim?” in Spanish?
faq.a: ¿Sabes nadar? if you are asking whether someone knows how. ¿Puedes nadar? if you are asking whether they are able to right now.

faq.q: How do you ask for permission in Spanish?
faq.a: Use poder: ¿Puedo pasar? (May I come in?) or, more politely, ¿Podría…?

¿___ hablar francés? (Do you speak French?)
